Why we are here

There are two ways to get LLMs wrong in research

CREDULOUS USE

“We used ChatGPT to code the responses.”

Paste data into a chat app, accept the answer, report the results. No record of the instrument, no validation, no idea where the data went.

REFLEXIVE DISMISSAL

“It's just autocomplete. It can't do real research work.”

Ruled out after one unhelpful chat session, while the evidence shows it matches trained coders on many well-specified tasks.

Treat it as an instrument: specify · constrain · validate · report
Both mistakes come from not knowing what the model is. That is today.

Why we are here · the evidence

How did the models perform and why?

WHERE IT HOLDS UP

Clear, closed categoriesa codebook a trained coder could follow
Short textsanswers, tweets, single statements
Checked against human codingevery study on the last slide did this

WHERE IT SLIPS

Rare and residual codes“other” and “no reason”: F1 of 0.02–0.3 out of the box
Long textsfull news articles: accuracy fell to 76–80%
Sizes and subtle riskseffects ~2× too large; social-desirability risks missed
0.94–1.00run-to-run ICC
The model gave the same codes when asked again: reliable.
≈ 0.7macro-F1 vs human codes
Out of the box, many of those codes were wrong: not yet valid.
von der Heyde et al. 2025 · 5,072 German open-ended answers
Model: GPT-4o

▲ un · answer · able
shares the root “answer” with answer, answers, answerable…
▲ rere · ad (dashed)
splits are statistical, not linguistic
+ advantages

02 Training · the pipeline

A model passes through several training stages

Pre-training
DATA
Web, books, code, papers
CHANGES
Learns to predict the next token
LEAVES IN OUTPUTS
Knowledge, gaps, text style
Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
DATA
Instruction and response pairs
CHANGES
Learns to answer, not continue
LEAVES IN OUTPUTS
Format, tone, refusals
Preference tuning: RLHF / DPO
DATA
People's choices between answers
CHANGES
Pushed towards preferred answers
LEAVES IN OUTPUTS
Politeness, agreeableness, lean
RL with verifiable rewards (RLVR)
DATA
Tasks with a checkable answer
CHANGES
Rewarded for correct results
LEAVES IN OUTPUTS
Step-by-step reasoning habits
Distillationside branch: a smaller model, made from a bigger one
DATA
A larger model's outputs
CHANGES
Small model learns to imitate
LEAVES IN OUTPUTS
The teacher's strengths and habits
Each stage is designed by trainers but not shared with end user.

TRUE NEXT TOKEN
" with"

then the window moves on

Base model

Assistant

02 Training · distillation

Distillation trains a small model to imitate a large one

Large teacher model
Small student model

Learning from its text

DeepSeek-R1-Distill: Qwen and Llama students, 1.5B to 70B, tuned on about 800k teacher samples.

Learning from its probabilities

Gemma 2 (2B, 9B). Llama 3.2 (1B, 3B): pruned from Llama 3.1 8B, then taught with logits from 8B and 70B.

Reported by Anthropic  Anthropic says (Feb 2026) three labs used ~24,000 fraudulent accounts and 16M+ exchanges to distil Claude.
Small models inherit their teacher's strengths and habits.

02 Training · opinions

Tuning moved models' expressed opinions away from training. No model is representative of the public

SANTURKAR ET AL. · ICML 2023 · 2022 MODELS

Human-feedback tuning widened the gap

Base models best matched moderate to conservative groups. OpenAI's tuned models matched liberal, high-income, educated groups. Asking a model to answer as a group helped only modestly.

ROZADO · PLOS ONE 2024

Most chat models lean left of centre

24 chat models, 11 political tests. A little extra fine-tuning moved a model left or right.

CERON ET AL. 2025 · PREPRINT

Where the lean starts is contested

Training data were left-skewed at both stages.

Opinions in a model are a product of training choices, and can be tuned.

02 Training · silicon samples

Simulated respondents: matches on averages, trouble with structure and spread

Where it has matched human data

ARGYLE ET AL. 2023 · GPT-3

US vote choice by subgroup: correlation 0.90 to 0.94 with ANES.

ASHOKKUMAR ET AL. 2026 · NATURE

Predicted 70 survey-experiment effects: r = 0.85, but sizes about 2× too big.

PARK ET AL. 2024 · PREPRINT

Agents built from interviews: 69% of GSS answers right, against 60% from demographics (people's own retest: 80%).

Where it fails

BISBEE ET AL. 2024 · POLITICAL ANALYSIS

Spread of answers about 0.6 of the real survey's; 48% of regression coefficients differed.

CUMMINS 2026 · AMPPS

252 defensible set-ups gave very different fidelity to humans.

WANG ET AL. 2025 · NAT. MACH. INTELL.

Models misportray and flatten identity groups.

Useful for piloting and hypothesis generation; not a substitute for respondents.

02 Training · a caution on simulated respondents

Barrie & Cerina (2026): Persona answers form belief systems that are too coherent

Real respondents (GSS)
DESIGN

28 LLMs, each given 1,000 persona biographies from the 2024 GSS, answered 52 attitude items.

FINDING

Persona answers were more tightly constrained than real respondents': more of the variance sits on one dimension.

CAUSE

Not identified. Mixture of open and closed weights models tested. Traits act as a strong prior over issue positions.

HOW TO READ THE AXIS
Share of variation on one dimension: higher = more one-dimensional. Each row is one model.
Matching averages can hide a flattened belief structure.

The provider's own bugs

Anthropic postmortem · Aug to Sep 2025
16%of Sonnet 4 requests hit a routing bug (worst hour, 31 Aug)

03 Where models run · quantisation

Quantisation: fewer bits per weight, smaller files, some losses

16-bit (bf16) · very fine gridstored as ·
8-bit · 256 levelsstored as ·
4-bit · only 16 levelsstored as ·
70B-parameter model, weights only
16-bit
140 GB
8-bit
70 GB
4-bit
35 GB

8-bit: close to lossless

Float 8-bit: effectively lossless. Integer 8-bit: 1 to 3% loss.

Kurtic et al. · 500,000+ evaluations

4-bit: fine on average, worse on long inputs

Drops of up to 59% on long-context tasks.

Mekala et al. 2025

Averages hid the damage

Japanese: 1.7% drop on automatic tasks, 16.0% in human evaluation.

Marchisio et al. 2024
Averages hide losses in long inputs and non-English text. OpenRouter let's you filter providers by quantisation levels for open-weight models.

R · ellmer
library(ellmer) chat <- chat_openrouter( model = "anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5", system_prompt = "Code as positive, negative, mixed or unclear." ) type_code <- type_object( code = type_enum(c("positive", "negative", "mixed", "unclear")), evidence = type_string() ) chat$chat_structured("The service was fine …", type = type_code)
PYTHON · openai
import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI(base_url="https://openrouter.ai/api/v1", api_key=os.environ["OPENROUTER_API_KEY"]) r = client.chat.completions.create( model="anthropic/claude-sonnet-5.5", messages=[ {"role": "system", "content": "Code: positive, …"}, {"role": "user", "content": "The service was fine …"}], ) print(r.choices[0].message.content) print(r.usage, r.choices[0].finish_reason)

04 Interacting · structured outputs

Constrained decoding masks any token that would break the schema

SO FAR:
{"code":"mixed
1Model scores every token
2Schema masks the invalid ones
3The rest are renormalised
4One is picked. Repeat.
Provider's inference engine performs constrained decoding, giving unallowed tokens 0 probability. SDK helps us configure it. Major APIs support structured outputs natively.

04 Interacting · reasoning models

A reasoning trace is not an explanation

BIASED PROMPTS
up to 36%accuracy drop

Hints change answers; the written reasoning rationalises them.

Example hint: the correct option is always “(A)” in the examples.

Turpin et al. 2023
A HINT THE MODEL USED
25% · 39%mentioned in the reasoning

Claude 3.7 Sonnet · DeepSeek R1

The hint changed the answer, but most reasoning never said so.

Chen et al. (Anthropic) 2025
A REWARD HACK THE MODEL USED
>99% → <2%used → mentioned

Exploited in nearly every case, admitted in almost none.

In 5 of 6 test environments.

Chen et al. (Anthropic) 2025
Reasoning traces are text generated after or alongside the decision, not explanation of inner process.

05 Reproducibility · why temperature 0 is not enough, 1 of 2

Floating-point addition is not associative, so the order changes the answer

FLOATING-POINT ADDITION · COMPUTED LIVE IN YOUR BROWSER
(0.1 + 1e20) − 1e20 = 0.1 + (1e20 − 1e20) =
Same numbers, different grouping, different answer.
TWO NEAR-TIED NEXT TOKENS

RUN A

" Agree"50.02%
" Disagree"49.98%

RUN B · last digits differ

" Agree"49.99%
" Disagree"50.01%
Temperature 0 takes the top token. The top token changed.
A last-digit difference can change the top token, and every token after it.

05 Reproducibility · why temperature 0 is not enough, 2 of 2

Your request shares a GPU with strangers, and that changes the arithmetic

different last digits→different logits→near-tie flips→different completion
Batch-invariant kernels: one fixed grouping, whatever the batch
1,000 / 1,000identical (Qwen3-235B, same prompt)
26 s → 42 sspeed cost (separate test, Qwen-3-8B, one GPU)
Determinism is possible only if you control the serving stack.
